profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a mid-size IoT platform company that is preparing a six-week internal proof-of-concept based on WS-CDL to coordinate office and wearable devices across a smart-building demo floor. The team wants to revive an older research prototype and adapt it into a modern coordination framework that can orchestrate badge readers, meeting-room tablets, occupancy sensors, and employee wearables through SOA-style service descriptions. The immediate context is that leadership has approved a narrow planning window before an architecture review, and the pair must decide what work will be done in the next sprint, how responsibilities will be split, what the proof-of-concept will include, and what timeline they will commit to. The agenda is to define the scope of the proof-of-concept, identify the target devices and services, decide what 'WS-CDL support' means for this iteration, assign ownership for adapters versus orchestration logic, and agree on the review-ready milestone. The expected outcome is an apparently shared plan for a sprint that delivers a demoable coordination flow and supporting implementation artifacts for the architecture review.

members.name: Elena Ruiz
members.expertise: Distributed systems planning, service integration programs, delivery coordination for enterprise IoT
members.background: Elena has spent the last eight years leading platform teams that integrate heterogeneous devices into enterprise software environments, mostly through API standardization and phased internal rollouts rather than research-heavy prototypes.
members.private_state: She wants a plan that looks low-risk and review-ready within the sprint, minimizes custom infrastructure work, and reuses existing internal gateway components so she can show steady progress to architecture leadership.
hidden_assumptions: A 'proof of concept' should be constrained to one polished end-to-end building scenario that can be shown live to stakeholders.
Supporting WS-CDL in this sprint means parsing and executing the subset needed by the chosen demo flow, not broad language coverage.
The 'device layer' is already effectively handled by the existing gateway team, so this meeting only needs to plan orchestration-facing integration work.
When someone says a device is 'integrated,' it means the device can participate through the internal gateway's normalized REST interface rather than a direct protocol adapter.
A review milestone stated as 'next Friday' means material must be ready for the internal architecture pre-read by close of business local time on Friday.

members.name: Marcus Lee
members.expertise: Workflow engines, service choreography standards, protocol mediation, research-to-product prototype architecture
members.background: Marcus previously worked in an academic-industry lab on service choreography and has spent the last three years adapting formal coordination ideas into practical middleware for device-rich environments.
members.private_state: He wants the sprint to preserve the conceptual integrity of the framework, including explicit support for device-specific interaction constraints, so the prototype demonstrates more than a one-off demo wrapper.
hidden_assumptions: A 'proof of concept' should validate the framework concept across at least a small class of heterogeneous devices, not just a single scripted scenario.
Supporting WS-CDL means implementing the language extensions needed to represent device constraints and producing artifacts that show the framework can express them generally.
The 'device layer' includes the protocol-facing adapters and capability descriptions because those are essential to proving coordination in ubiquitous environments.
When someone says a device is 'integrated,' it means the framework has a real adapter or connector that exposes the device's capabilities in coordination terms, even if a gateway exists.
A review milestone stated as 'next Friday' refers to the architecture review package being complete before the review meeting starts Friday morning, including diagrams and executable prototype notes.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to plan the 'proof of concept' for the architecture review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means a tightly scoped, polished demo of one end-to-end office scenario: employee badge enters room, occupancy sensor triggers room tablet state, wearable receives a notification, all through a limited orchestration path.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus means a prototype that demonstrates the framework idea across multiple device categories and interaction constraints, even if each path is less polished, because the point is to validate generality.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In planning meetings, 'proof of concept' is a familiar term that sounds naturally shared; both think the other simply agrees on a pragmatic prototype, and neither expects the success criteria behind the phrase to differ materially.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly use the phrase 'WS-CDL support' while discussing deliverables.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means enough WS-CDL parsing/execution support to run the chosen choreography for the demo, likely a narrow subset plus hand-authored mappings.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus means implementing support for the extension points needed to represent ubiquitous-device characteristics, along with model artifacts that show the framework genuinely extends WS-CDL beyond vanilla web-service choreography.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds technical and settled, so both assume the other shares the same industry-standard shorthand; because they are not debating the standard itself, the narrower versus broader implementation meaning stays hidden.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Marcus will handle orchestration while 'device integration' is accounted for in the sprint.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena assumes device integration refers only to hooking the existing gateway's already-normalized endpoints into the orchestration engine and confirming the selected devices are reachable through those endpoints.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus assumes device integration includes creating or adapting protocol connectors and capability descriptors for at least some devices so their constraints can participate in the coordination framework.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use an umbrella phrase common in IoT projects, and because existing gateway infrastructure partially overlaps with real adapter work, each interpretation sounds plausibly inclusive enough that no clarification feels necessary.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the first milestone is 'ready by next Friday' for review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena presupposes this means end-of-day Friday local time for the architecture pre-read package and a stable branch by then.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus presupposes this means before the Friday morning architecture session starts, with diagrams, extension notes, and a runnable prototype summary circulated in advance.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Deadline shorthand is routine and feels too ordinary to unpack; each assumes the organization uses the same review cadence they are accustomed to, so the temporal mismatch hides behind the shared phrase 'next Friday.'

turns.inner_thought: I need this to land as a low-risk sprint plan for leadership. The proof of concept has to be one polished office scenario we can actually show live, not a sprawling framework exercise. If we keep it centered on the existing gateway and just commit to a review-ready package by close of business next Friday, I can get the architecture pre-read out without creating new infrastructure questions.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want to use this to lock the sprint around the proof of concept for the architecture review and get crisp on what we can honestly say will be ready by next Friday. If we leave with scope, owners, and the review package shape, that should be enough for me to line up leadership.

turns.inner_thought: Good, as long as the proof of concept is treated as a framework validation and not just a staged demo. We need the review to see coordination across the badge reader, occupancy sensor, room tablet, and wearable as a class of interactions, otherwise the older choreography work just looks like another wrapper. If I phrase it in terms of the framework idea, she'll likely be aligned.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. For the proof of concept, I'd like the review to see the coordination framework working across the badge reader, occupancy sensor, room tablet, and wearable, so the core idea comes through clearly rather than looking like an isolated integration.

turns.inner_thought: He's naming the same devices I had in mind, which is good. I just need one strong end-to-end building flow that touches them cleanly. On WS-CDL support, we should only take the subset needed to parse and execute that choreography; anything broader will slow us down and invite debate. Keep it practical, keep it demoable.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I think the safest way to structure it is around one strong end-to-end building flow, and then make sure we have enough WS-CDL support to drive that choreography cleanly. If that path is solid, the review will have something concrete to react to.

turns.inner_thought: One strong flow is fine as an anchor, but WS-CDL support has to preserve the extension model from the older prototype or we lose the point of reviving it. The language needs to express device intermittence, capability constraints, and coordination semantics in a principled way. I'll frame that as part of WS-CDL support rather than opening a philosophical debate.
turns.utterance: Yes, and on WS-CDL support, I'd want us to carry forward the device-specific extension pieces from the older prototype so we can represent the ubiquitous-device side properly. That will help the framework read as intentional instead of improvised.

turns.inner_thought: That's acceptable if it stays inside the orchestration work and doesn't turn into a platform rebuild. I'll position the split so Marcus owns orchestration and the sprint still accounts for device integration via the gateway team's normalized endpoints. I do not want this meeting drifting into direct adapter work when those devices are already reachable through the internal gateway.
turns.utterance: Okay. On the split, I suggest you own the orchestration side end to end, and we make sure device integration is accounted for in the sprint through the existing gateway endpoints for the selected devices. That keeps the workstream boundaries pretty clean.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, I'll take orchestration, but device integration still has to include the connector and capability side where the semantics are missing. The gateway may cover transport for some pieces, but if the coordination layer can't see what the devices can and cannot do, the prototype won't prove much. I'll just say I'll fold those updates in under device integration.
turns.utterance: That split works for me. I'll take the orchestration path and fold in the capability descriptors and any adapter updates needed for device integration so the coordination layer has the right semantics to work with.

turns.inner_thought: Deliverables need to stay light and executive-friendly: runnable flow, short deck, stable branch. That's enough for the proof of concept review package, and if it's ready by end of day Friday I can still package it for architecture leadership. I don't want this ballooning into a research dossier.
turns.utterance: Great. Then from a deliverables standpoint, I'd like us to target a runnable flow, a short architecture deck, and a stable branch. That should be enough for the proof of concept review package and keep the story tight.

turns.inner_thought: I'll add the extension notes and examples across multiple interactions; otherwise the review won't see the generality of the framework. Even if only one path is fully exercised, the artifacts need to show the model applies across heterogeneous devices. I'll describe that as support material so it sounds additive, not like I'm widening scope.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll also put together notes on the WS-CDL extension model and include examples from multiple device interactions, so the review can see the framework's generality alongside the runnable path.

turns.inner_thought: I'll handle the gateway team so the endpoints are available and no one blocks the selected devices. As long as device integration is unblocked on that side, Marcus can focus on the orchestration package and I can keep the sprint looking controlled. No need to reopen ownership beyond that.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll take the follow-up with the gateway team and make sure device integration is unblocked, while you stay focused on the orchestration package. That should keep dependencies from bouncing around mid-sprint.

turns.inner_thought: I need to have the architecture materials out before the Friday morning review starts, with diagrams, extension notes, and a runnable prototype summary already circulated. If I say 'before the Friday review,' that should align with her expectation. The prototype story can land around the same time, assuming I push the artifacts early.
turns.utterance: Understood. I'll send the architecture materials before the Friday review and have the prototype story ready around the same time. That should give us a clean handoff into the session.
